lesson.title: The Formula Behind the Rate: Unpacking the Difference Quotient
lesson.summary: The difference quotient rewrites average rate of change as a single algebraic expression in terms of x and a step size h, turning a numerical calculation into a formula that can be simplified once and reused for any interval.
lesson.body:
The average rate of change of f from x to x+h is [f(x+h) - f(x)] divided by h. Written this way, with a general starting point x and a general step size h rather than two specific numbers a and b, this expression is called the difference quotient. It is exactly the same quantity as average rate of change, just expressed algebraically so that it can be simplified symbolically before any specific numbers are plugged in, which is essential for finding instantaneous rates by letting h shrink toward 0.

Find the difference quotient for f(x) = x^2 + 3x. First compute f(x+h) by substituting x+h everywhere x appears: f(x+h) = (x+h)^2 + 3(x+h) = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h. Next subtract f(x) = x^2 + 3x: f(x+h) - f(x) = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h) - (x^2 + 3x) = 2xh + h^2 + 3h. Every remaining term has a factor of h, so factor it out: 2xh + h^2 + 3h = h(2x + h + 3). Finally divide by h, which is valid as long as h is not exactly 0: [f(x+h) - f(x)] divided by h = 2x + h + 3.

Verify this simplified formula against direct computation. Let x=1 and h=0.1. Direct computation: f(1) = 1 + 3 = 4, and f(1.1) = 1.21 + 3.3 = 4.51, so [f(1.1) - f(1)] divided by 0.1 = 0.51/0.1 = 5.1. Now check the simplified formula: 2x + h + 3 with x=1 and h=0.1 gives 2(1) + 0.1 + 3 = 5.1. The two methods agree exactly, confirming the algebra was done correctly.

The same method extends to higher-degree functions with more algebra but no new ideas. For f(x) = x^3, expand f(x+h) = (x+h)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3, using the binomial expansion. Subtracting f(x) = x^3 leaves 3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3, and every term again carries a factor of h, so dividing by h gives the difference quotient 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2. Letting h approach 0 leaves 3x^2, meaning the instantaneous rate of change of x^3 at any point x is 3x^2; at x=2, for instance, that predicts an instantaneous rate of 3(4) = 12, a value that could be checked numerically the same way the x^2 example was checked in the previous section.

The value of simplifying the difference quotient before substituting numbers is that the factor of h in the denominator can be cancelled algebraically, which is impossible to do after h has already been set to a specific decimal value. Once the quotient is reduced to 2x + h + 3, it becomes clear what happens as h shrinks toward 0: the expression approaches 2x + 3, with no division by zero ever actually occurring, because the cancellation happened before the limit was taken. This is the general pattern used to compute the instantaneous rate of change at every point x at once, rather than one point at a time as in the previous section.

The difference quotient is therefore the algebraic engine sitting underneath both average rate of change and instantaneous rate of change: average rate of change is the difference quotient evaluated at one specific h corresponding to the width of a chosen interval, and instantaneous rate of change is the limit of the difference quotient as h approaches 0. The same expression, viewed two different ways, produces both quantities.
